bibliography.abstract: Assessment in Geographic Information Systems (GIS) education is complex, as student work combines technical implementation, spatial reasoning, interpretation, and visual communication. While large language models (LLMs) are increasingly discussed in higher education, empirical evidence on their role in assessment remains limited. This study addresses a sensitive issue many instructors have considered yet remains cautiously discussed: whether LLMs can responsibly support grading. Using a comparative design, we analyzed manual and LLM-based grading across three master-level courses: programming-based spatial analysis, interpretative GIS, and cartography. Identical course-specific rubrics were provided to an instructor and the LLM. Outcomes were compared in terms of grades, grading time, and feedback length, alongside qualitative analysis of feedback structure. Results show high agreement in relative student rankings, although alignment varied across course types. Agreement in absolute grades was closer in interpretative courses, while larger differences emerged in programming tasks, where the LLM graded more strictly. Feedback was generally more detailed, and model execution time per submission was substantially lower than manual grading time. The findings support a constrained, rubric-driven role for LLMs as structured assessment support within instructor-led workflows. Responsible implementation requires transparency, instructor oversight, and reproducible evaluation procedures. Further research is needed before broader adoption in education.

en.caveats: The evaluation was limited to three specific master-level courses, and the degree of grading alignment varied significantly depending on the course type.
en.what: This study evaluated the performance of a Large Language Model (LLM) against a human instructor in grading student work across three master-level GIS courses covering programming-based spatial analysis, interpretative GIS, and cartography. Using identical course-specific rubrics, the evaluation compared absolute grades, relative student rankings, grading time, and feedback length. The LLM demonstrated high agreement with the instructor on relative student rankings, graded more strictly on programming tasks, and generated longer, more detailed feedback in a fraction of the manual grading time.
en.why: It establishes that LLMs can reliably assist with structured, rubric-driven grading in GIS education, shifting the technology from a suspected source of academic misconduct to a viable tool for reducing instructor grading workloads.
